Special Recreational Vessels Bill 2019 - Second Reading - Support Australia's shipping industry

The Special Recreational Vessels Bill was moved for second reading, allowing foreign special recreational vessels to apply for a temporary licence to operate on the Australian coast for hire or charter, with the industry expecting a large number of vessels for the Tokyo Olympics and Americas Cup in Auckland, and broader economic benefits anticipated for Australian businesses, particularly in regional areas.

The speaker supported the Special Recreational Vessels Bill 2019 with Labor-negotiated amendments including a sunset clause until June 2021, a ban on commercial cargo carriage, and confirmation that crews receive Australian wages and conditions, while criticising the government for undermining the Australian shipping industry.

The Special Recreational Vessels Bill 2019 was argued to allow superyachts to obtain temporary coastal trading licences for charter services, aiming to unlock 11,800 jobs and over $1.5 billion by 2020-21, while criticising the current Coastal Trading Act for excluding these vessels and costing the economy millions.

The speaker argued for the Special Recreational Vessels Bill 2019, which would allow foreign superyachts to obtain a temporary trading licence for commercial charters in Australian waters for up to 12 months, aiming to capture a share of the global superyacht market and create approximately 12,000 new skilled jobs. The bill would remove barriers such as import duties and the minimum five-voyage requirement under the current coastal trading act, unlocking economic benefits for businesses like Rivergate Marina and Riviera.

The Special Recreational Vessels Bill 2019 will allow special recreational vessels to apply for temporary licences for single-voyage charters to and from the same port, opening up a new maritime market and boosting tourism in regional areas like Far North Queensland, while maintaining protections for Australian vessels and prohibiting cargo for profit.
